Fix \(\theta\in\Theta\) and \(k\geq 2\).  Put
\[
 v_k=\alpha^k u_k,
 \qquad
 w_k=\bigl(\kappa_k(\epsilon_{t,e})-\kappa_k(\epsilon_{t,0})\bigr)_{e=1}^{E-1}.
\]
The source moment generating functions are finite in a neighborhood of zero, so the relevant cumulants exist.  By source independence, the joint moment generating function of \(\alpha U_e\) and \(\epsilon_{t,e}\) factorizes.  Taking the degree-\(k\) derivative of its logarithm gives additivity of cumulants of independent sums, and hence, by the definition of \(c_k\),
\[
 c_k=v_k+w_k=\alpha^k u_k+w_k. \tag{1}
\]
Multilinearity of the joint cumulant and the structural equation for \(Y_e\) give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \kappa_k(Y_e,T_e,\ldots,T_e)
 &=\beta\kappa_k(T_e)
   +\gamma\kappa_k(U_e,T_e,\ldots,T_e)
   +\kappa_k(\epsilon_y,T_e,\ldots,T_e).
 \end{aligned}                                       \tag{2}
\]
The last term in (2) is zero because \(\epsilon_y\) is independent of \(T_e\) and \(k\geq2\).  On expanding each of the remaining \(k-1\) arguments \(T_e=\alpha U_e+\epsilon_{t,e}\), every term containing both \(U_e\) and \(\epsilon_{t,e}\) is a mixed cumulant of independent groups and is zero.  Thus
\[
 \kappa_k(U_e,T_e,\ldots,T_e)=\alpha^{k-1}\kappa_k(U_e)
 =\alpha^{k-1}\kappa_k(\epsilon_{u,e}).              \tag{3}
\]
Subtracting the environment-zero version of (2), and using (3) and the definitions of \(m_k,c_k,u_k\), yields
\[
 m_k-\beta c_k=\alpha^{k-1}\gamma u_k.              \tag{4}
\]
The latent-profile-plane assumption gives \(u_k\in A\), so (4) lies in \(A\).  The calibration-rank assumption makes the displayed formula for \(Q_A\) well defined, and that formula is the orthogonal projector with kernel \(A\).  Applying it to (4) proves
\[
 Q_A m_k=\beta Q_Ac_k,
\]
as asserted.

For a Poisson variable \(N\) of intensity \(\lambda\), the centered variable \(j(N-\lambda)\) has log moment generating function
\[
 \lambda\{\exp(jt)-1-jt\}.
\]
Consequently its cumulant of every order \(k\geq2\) is \(\lambda j^k\).  Independence over \(j\) and additivity of log moment generating functions therefore give, for the witness in the definition,
\[
 u_k
 =\eta(1^k,2^k,\ldots,d^k,0,\ldots,0)^\top.       \tag{5}
\]
The treatment Gaussian has the same law in every environment and \(\alpha=1\), so its cumulant contrasts vanish and (1) gives \(c_k=u_k\).  In particular,
\[
 C=\begin{bmatrix}\eta V_d\\0\end{bmatrix}.         \tag{6}
\]
To verify nonsingularity without invoking an undeclared result, factor \(j^2\) from row \(j\) of \(V_d\).  The remaining matrix has entries \(j^{k-2}\), with exponents \(0,\ldots,d-1\).  If a linear combination of its columns were zero, the resulting polynomial of degree at most \(d-1\) would vanish at the \(d\) distinct points \(1,\ldots,d\), and hence would be the zero polynomial.  Thus \(V_d\) is nonsingular.  Equation (6) also gives
\[
 C^\top C=\eta^2V_d^\top V_d,
 \qquad
 \sigma_d(C)=\eta\sigma_d(V_d)\geq\kappa_0+\rho.    \tag{7}
\]
It follows from (6) that
\[
 A=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf e_1,\ldots,\mathbf e_d\}.
\]
Equation (5) places every \(c_k\) and every \(u_k\) in this plane, so \(Q_Ac_k=0\) for every \(k\geq2\) and \(r^\star(\theta)=\infty\).

All constructed sources are centered.  They are mutually independent by construction, and their moment generating functions are entire because they are finite sums of bounded-jump compound-Poisson variables and Gaussians.  The displayed feasibility inequality supplies the required \((2R_{\max}+\delta)\)-moment bound with \(\rho\) slack.  The coefficient inequalities in the witness supply, separately, the effect, loading, and confounding bounds with \(\rho\) slack.  Equations (6)--(7) supply calibration rank, calibration gap, and the latent-profile condition.  Hence \(\theta\in\Theta_\rho^\circ\).

Write \(V_e=\epsilon_{u,e}\) and \(W_e=\epsilon_{t,e}\).  For the original representation,
\[
 T_e=V_e+W_e,
 \qquad
 Y_e=-\frac q2(V_e+W_e)+qV_e+\epsilon_y
     =\frac q2V_e-\frac q2W_e+\epsilon_y.             \tag{8}
\]
The source swap has coefficients \((1,q/2,-q)\), latent source \(W_e\), and treatment source \(V_e\).  Direct substitution gives exactly the two random variables in (8), on the same probability space.  Thus it induces the same \(P_e\) in every environment.  Its latent source has no environmental cumulant contrast because the \(W_e\) have a common Gaussian law.  Its observed \(C,A,Q_A\), and hence its value of \(r^\star\), are unchanged.  Since \(\alpha=1\), swapping the two source families preserves the moment slack; the effect and confounding magnitudes are respectively \(q/2\) and \(q\), and all remaining coefficient and calibration inequalities have already been checked.  Therefore \(S\theta\in\Theta_\rho^\circ\) and \(r^\star(S\theta)=\infty\).  The definition of \(\mathcal N_\rho\) now gives \(\theta\in\mathcal N_\rho\), while (8) shows that the two legal effects are \(-q/2\) and \(q/2\).  This also proves nonemptiness under exactly the feasibility conditions stated in the proposition.

Let \(\theta\in\mathcal B\).  By definition, \(r^\star\leq R_{\max}<\infty\), so at least one \(k\) has \(Q_Ac_k\neq0\).  The cumulant-cancellation lemma gives \(Q_Am_k=\beta Q_Ac_k\), and taking the Euclidean inner product with \(Q_Ac_k\) yields
\[
 \beta=\frac{\langle Q_Ac_k,Q_Am_k\rangle}
 {\lVert Q_Ac_k\rVert_2^2}.                          \tag{9}
\]
Every quantity on the right of (9) is a functional of the observed laws: cumulants give \(c_k,m_k\), the first \(d\) treatment contrasts give \(C\), and the calibration-rank assumption gives \(Q_A\).

To prove identification rather than merely derive a moment equation, let \(\widetilde\theta\in\mathcal D_\rho\) induce the same collection of observed laws.  Then it has the same \(c_k,m_k,C,A,Q_A\), and \(r^\star\).  In particular its breakout is finite, so the disjoint definition of the two branches places \(\widetilde\theta\) in \(\mathcal B\).  Applying (9) to \(\widetilde\theta\) gives \(\widetilde\beta=\beta\).  Thus \(\beta\) is identified relative to the full domain at every point of \(\mathcal B\).

Now let \(\theta\in\mathcal N_\rho\), and set
\[
 V_e=\alpha\epsilon_{u,e},\qquad W_e=\epsilon_{t,e},
 \qquad q=\gamma/\alpha.
\]
The treatment-loading lower bound permits the division by \(\alpha\).  The observed variables can be written
\[
 T_e=V_e+W_e,
 \qquad
 Y_e=(\beta+q)V_e+\beta W_e+\epsilon_y.              \tag{10}
\]
Under \(S\theta\), the latent and treatment sources are \(W_e\) and \(V_e\), while the coefficients are \(1,\beta+q,-q\).  Hence
\[
 T'_e=W_e+V_e,\qquad
 Y'_e=(\beta+q)(W_e+V_e)-qW_e+\epsilon_y
      =(\beta+q)V_e+\beta W_e+\epsilon_y.            \tag{11}
\]
Equations (10)--(11) prove equality of the complete observed laws, not only equality of their moments.  The definition of \(\mathcal N_\rho\) already supplies \(S\theta\in\Theta_\rho^\circ\) and \(r^\star(S\theta)=\infty\).  For completeness, it also implies that \(S\theta\) itself belongs to \(\mathcal N_\rho\).  Indeed,
\[
 S^2\theta=(1,\beta,\gamma/\alpha,
             \{\alpha\epsilon_{u,e},\epsilon_{t,e}\}_{e\in\mathcal E},
             \epsilon_y).                            \tag{12}
\]
The loading value one is legal because it is the loading of \(S\theta\); the effect and confounding bounds in (12) are inherited from \(\theta\); and the two source families in (12) are exactly the two source families of \(S\theta\) in the opposite order, so their centeredness, independence, entire moment generating functions, and moment bounds are inherited.  Its latent contrasts are \(\alpha^k u_k\in A\), and its observed laws, calibration gap, and infinite breakout are unchanged by (10)--(11).  Thus \(S^2\theta\in\Theta_\rho^\circ\) with infinite breakout, proving \(S\theta\in\mathcal N_\rho\subset\mathcal D_\rho\).

Finally, the two effects differ by \(q=\gamma/\alpha\), whose magnitude is at least \(q_0>0\).  Therefore no observed-law functional can equal both, and \(\beta\) is not identified at any point of \(\mathcal N_\rho\).  Since \(\mathcal D_\rho=\mathcal B\cup\mathcal N_\rho\), the two arguments prove the claimed if-and-only-if frontier.  The final comparison in the statement adds no mathematical premise: the swap algebra is already explicit in (10)--(11), whereas (9) uses the joint environmental plane and a nonzero complementary direction, which requires the multi-environment geometry proved below.

The columns of \(C\) lie in \(\mathbb R^{E-1}\).  Thus \(\operatorname{rank}(C)=d\) implies \(d\leq E-1\).  If \(E=d+1\), then \(C\) has rank \(d\) in \(\mathbb R^d\), so
\[
 A=\operatorname{col}(C)=\mathbb R^d,
 \qquad Q_A=0.                                      \tag{13}
\]
Consequently no projected contrast can be nonzero.  More generally, a finite breakout requires \(A^\perp\neq\{0\}\), hence \(d<E-1\), which is equivalent to \(E\geq d+2\).

We now prove attainability at every prescribed order with one collection of bounds.  Fix \(d\geq1\), \(E\geq d+2\), and \(R_{\max}\geq d+2\).  For \(r\in\{d+2,\ldots,R_{\max}\}\), define
\[
 \nu_{rj}=(-1)^{r-j}\binom{r}{j},\qquad 1\leq j\leq r.
\]
The binomial identity
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^r(-1)^{r-j}\binom{r}{j}e^{jt}=(e^t-1)^r                 \tag{14}
\]
shows, after taking \(k\) derivatives at zero, that
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^r\nu_{rj}j^k=0\quad(0\leq k<r),
 \qquad
 \sum_{j=1}^r\nu_{rj}j^r=r!.                       \tag{15}
\]
The omitted \(j=0\) term is zero for \(k\geq1\), and (15) at \(k=0\) follows directly from (14).

Choose \(L,\eta>0\), put
\[
 K_\nu=\max_{d+2\leq s\leq R_{\max}}\max_{1\leq j\leq s}|\nu_{sj}|,
 \qquad 0<\varepsilon<L/(2K_\nu),                    \tag{16}
\]
and use the environment \(e=d+1\) as a spare coordinate.  Let \(\epsilon_{u,e}\) be a centered compound-Poisson sum having jumps \(1,\ldots,d\), baseline intensity \(L\) at every jump, and, only in environment \(e=j\leq d\), an additional intensity \(\eta\) at jump \(j\).  Add an independent centered Gaussian if desired.  Let \(\epsilon_{t,e}\) have jumps \(1,\ldots,R_{\max}\), all with baseline intensity \(L\), except that in the spare environment its jump-\(j\) intensity is \(L+\varepsilon\nu_{rj}\) for \(j\leq r\).  Again add a common independent Gaussian.  All remaining environments have baseline intensities.  Inequality (16) makes every intensity at least \(L/2>0\).  Take \(\epsilon_y\) Gaussian and all source families mutually independent, and set \(\alpha=1\), \(\beta=0\), and \(\gamma=1\).

The compound-Poisson log moment generating function calculation used above and (15) give
\[
 u_k=\eta(1^k,\ldots,d^k,0,\ldots,0)^\top,
 \qquad
 c_k=u_k+\varepsilon\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^r\nu_{rj}j^k\right)\mathbf e_{d+1}. \tag{17}
\]
Because \(r\geq d+2\), equations (15)--(17) imply
\[
 C=\begin{bmatrix}\eta V_d\\0\end{bmatrix},
 \quad
 A=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf e_1,\ldots,\mathbf e_d\},
 \quad
 Q_Ac_k=0\ (d+2\leq k<r),
 \quad
 Q_Ac_r=\varepsilon r!\,\mathbf e_{d+1}\neq0.        \tag{18}
\]
The polynomial-root argument in the proof of the nonvacuity proposition proves that \(V_d\) is nonsingular.  Hence the calibration rank is \(d\), and
\[
 \sigma_d(C)=\eta\sigma_d(V_d)>0.                    \tag{19}
\]
Equations (18)--(19) prove \(r^\star=r\) and the latent-profile restriction at every order.

All sources are centered and independent, and their moment generating functions are entire.  There are only finitely many values of \(r\), environments, and source families in the construction.  Therefore their absolute moments of order \(2R_{\max}+\delta\) have a finite maximum.  Choose \(M\) larger than that maximum and choose
\[
 0<\kappa_0<\eta\sigma_d(V_d).
\]
Choose once and for all coefficient bounds containing \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=(1,0,1)\), and choose all other fixed bounds large enough to contain the displayed finite family.  These choices do not depend on \(r\).  Thus the same finite \(M\), positive \(\kappa_0\), and remaining bounds make every construction legal, which proves the converse and hence sharpness.

We prove the proposed, explicitly quantified claim.  The qualification concerning a compatible fixed experiment is necessary because no lower feasibility relation between the arbitrary moment envelope and the arbitrary calibration gap is present in the frozen assumptions.

Fix \(d,E,R_{\max}\) as in the statement.  Let \(V_e,W_e\) and \(Z\) be mutually independent centered sources.  Give both \(V_e\) and \(W_e\) positive compound-Poisson baseline intensities \(L\) at jumps \(1,\ldots,R_{\max}\), as well as independent nondegenerate Gaussian components.  In environment \(e=j\leq d\), increase the jump-\(j\) intensity of \(V_e\) by \(\eta\) and that of \(W_e\) by \(2\eta\); leave every other intensity at baseline.  Let the invariant outcome source \(Z\) be Gaussian.  Before the order-specific perturbation, define two structural representations by
\[
 \begin{array}{c|ccc|cc}
 &\alpha&\beta&\gamma&\epsilon_{u,e}&\epsilon_{t,e}\\ \hline
 \theta_0^\circ&1&2&1&V_e&W_e\\
 \theta_1^\circ&1&3&-1&W_e&V_e.
 \end{array}                                                   \tag{20}
\]
They have identical observed variables on a common realization, since
\[
 T_e=V_e+W_e,\qquad Y_e=3V_e+2W_e+Z                         \tag{21}
\]
under both rows of (20).  Their calibration contrasts are
\[
 c_k=3\eta(1^k,\ldots,d^k,0,\ldots,0)^\top.                \tag{22}
\]

Fix \(r\in\{d+2,\ldots,R_{\max}\}\), and use the coefficients \(\nu_{rj}\) from (14)--(15).  In the spare environment \(e=d+1\), alter the jump-\(j\) intensity of the treatment source of \(\theta_0^\circ\), namely \(W_{d+1}\), by \(\varepsilon\nu_{rj}\).  Separately, alter the jump-\(j\) intensity of the treatment source of \(\theta_1^\circ\), namely \(V_{d+1}\), by the same amount.  Choose \(\varepsilon\) by (16), so every resulting intensity is positive.  Center each resulting compound-Poisson variable.  Denote the two altered structural parameters by \(\theta_0,\theta_1\).

For every source cumulant order \(s<r\), the alteration is zero by (15), while at order \(r\) it is \(\varepsilon r!\).  Hence all joint cumulants of \((T_e,Y_e)\) of total order below \(r\) equal their unaltered values: this follows directly by multilinearly expanding each joint cumulant in the independent sources in (20).  Those unaltered joint laws agree by (21).  To pass from cumulants to the asserted mixed moments, differentiate the identity between the joint moment generating function and the exponential of its cumulant generating function.  For \(s=p+\ell\), this gives the finite partition formula
\[
 \mathbb E[T_e^pY_e^\ell]
 =\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak P_s}\prod_{D\in\pi}
   \operatorname{cum}\bigl((X_i)_{i\in D}\bigr),             \tag{23}
\]
where \(X_1,\ldots,X_s\) consists of \(p\) copies of \(T_e\) and \(\ell\) copies of \(Y_e\).  Every block in (23) has size at most \(s<r\), so all factors, and therefore the moments, agree under \(\theta_0\) and \(\theta_1\).

The order-specific changes vanish through order \(d+1\), so (22) still determines \(C\) and
\[
 A=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf e_1,\ldots,\mathbf e_d\}.
\]
The latent profile of \(\theta_0\) has coordinate increments \(\eta j^k\), and that of \(\theta_1\) has coordinate increments \(2\eta j^k\); both lie in \(A\) at every order.  At the first nonvanishing spare-coordinate order,
\[
 \begin{array}{c|cc}
 &Q_Ac_r&Q_Am_r\\ \hline
 \theta_0&\varepsilon r!\,\mathbf e_{d+1}&2\varepsilon r!\,\mathbf e_{d+1}\\
 \theta_1&\varepsilon r!\,\mathbf e_{d+1}&3\varepsilon r!\,\mathbf e_{d+1}.
 \end{array}                                                   \tag{24}
\]
Thus both first breakouts equal \(r\), while their effects are \(2\) and \(3\).

The Vandermonde argument proves rank and a positive fixed gap for (22).  Positivity of all jump intensities proves realizability; finite jump support plus Gaussian convolution proves entire moment generating functions.  Since there are finitely many \(r\), choose one coefficient box containing the two rows of (20), one positive calibration gap below \(3\eta\sigma_d(V_d)\), and one finite moment envelope larger than the maximum source moment over all constructions.  These fixed choices make every \(\theta_0,\theta_1\) a member of \(\mathcal B\).  Finally, allowing \(L\) and the Gaussian variances to vary in sufficiently small nontrivial compact intervals preserves positivity, all strict inequalities, (22), and (24).  The resulting subclass is finite-dimensional and nondegenerate, completing the proof.

When \(d=1\) and \(E=2\), the matrix \(C\) has one row and one column.  The assumption \(\operatorname{rank}(C)=1\) says its column is nonzero, so
\[
 A=\operatorname{col}(C)=\mathbb R,
 \qquad
 Q_A=I_1-C(C^\top C)^{-1}C^\top=0.                  \tag{25}
\]
It follows from the definition of \(r^\star\) that \(r^\star=\infty\) for every calibrated parameter, and hence \(\mathcal B=\varnothing\).  Whenever a source-swap pair is legal, the identification-frontier theorem gives equality of its complete two-environment observed laws and distinct effects.  Thus the surviving branch has exactly the simultaneous-source label ambiguity stated in the proposition.  This is an algebraic derivation of the reduction; the comparison with Kivva et al., Theorem 3.6, is not used as a proof premise.

We prove the proposed claim in two parts.  The upper bounds are uniform over every fixed admissible bounded model.  The lower bounds are proved on one fixed compatible model, as the claim now says; mere nonemptiness under arbitrary numerical envelopes does not imply that a particular least-favorable family fits those envelopes.

\emph{Uniform cumulant estimation.}
Let \(s_0=2R_{\max}+\delta\).  The coefficient bounds imply
\[
 |\gamma|\leq a_1q_1.
\]
The structural equations, the source \(s_0\)-moment envelope, the triangle inequality in \(L^{s_0}\), and Lyapunov's inequality therefore give a constant \(K_0<\infty\), depending only on the fixed model bounds, such that
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\max_{e\in\mathcal E}
 \mathbb E_\theta\bigl(|T_e|^{s_0}+|Y_e|^{s_0}\bigr)\leq K_0. \tag{26}
\]
Here all divisions by \(\alpha\) are licensed by \(|\alpha|\geq a_0>0\).

For clarity, an unbiased joint-cumulant estimator can be written explicitly.  For variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_k\), each equal to \(T_e\) or \(Y_e\), the population identity obtained by differentiating the log moment generating function is
\[
 \operatorname{cum}(X_1,\ldots,X_k)
 =\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak P_k}(|\pi|-1)!(-1)^{|\pi|-1}
   \prod_{D\in\pi}\mathbb E\!\left[\prod_{j\in D}X_j\right]. \tag{27}
\]
For a partition \(\pi=\{D_1,\ldots,D_s\}\), replace its product of expectations by
\[
 \frac{1}{(n_e)_s}
 \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_s\ {
m distinct}}
 \prod_{a=1}^s\prod_{j\in D_a}X_{j,e,i_a}.           \tag{28}
\]
Independence of distinct observations shows directly that (28) is unbiased.  Symmetrizing (27)--(28) produces the stipulated cumulant U-statistics.  The square of every summand uses total degree at most \(2k\leq2R_{\max}<s_0\), so (26) and H\"older's inequality bound its second moment uniformly.  In the variance double sum, pairs of ordered index tuples with disjoint index sets have zero covariance; only \(O(n_e^{2s-1})\) of the \(O(n_e^{2s})\) pairs overlap.  Thus, for a uniform constant \(K_1\),
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta
 \left(\lVert\widehat c_k-c_k\rVert_2^2+
       \lVert\widehat m_k-m_k\rVert_2^2\right)
 \leq \frac{K_1}{n},
 \qquad 2\leq k\leq R_{\max},                       \tag{29}
\]
once \(n_e\geq R_{\max}\).  We used \(n_e\geq\underline\pi n\) and the fact that \(E,R_{\max}\) are fixed.  Formula (26) also bounds all population cumulants in (29), through (27).

Put \(H=\widehat C-C\).  On \(\lVert H\rVert_{\rm op}\leq\kappa_0/2\), every unit vector \(x=Cy\) in \(A\) has \(\lVert y\rVert\leq1/\kappa_0\), and hence lies within \(\lVert H\rVert_{\rm op}/\kappa_0\) of \(\operatorname{col}(\widehat C)\).  Conversely, the variational definition of the smallest singular value gives directly
\[
 \sigma_d(\widehat C)
 =\inf_{\lVert y\rVert=1}\lVert(C+H)y\rVert
 \geq\sigma_d(C)-\lVert H\rVert_{\rm op}
 \geq\kappa_0/2.
\]
The same approximation argument in the reverse direction therefore gives distance at most \(2\lVert H\rVert_{\rm op}/\kappa_0\).  Taking suprema over unit vectors in the two subspaces yields
\[
 \lVert\widehat Q-Q_A\rVert_{\rm op}
 \leq \frac{4}{\kappa_0}\lVert H\rVert_{\rm op}.    \tag{30}
\]
On the complementary event the left side is at most two, while Markov's inequality and (29) make that event's probability \(O(n^{-1})\).  Hence
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta
 \lVert\widehat Q-Q_A\rVert_{\rm op}^2\leq K_2/n.   \tag{31}
\]

For \(|b|\leq B\), define
\[
 g_k(b)=Q_A(m_k-bc_k),\qquad
 \widehat g_k(b)=\widehat Q(\widehat m_k-b\widehat c_k),
\]
and
\[
 \Delta_n=\max_{d+2\leq k\leq R_{\max}}
 \sup_{|b|\leq B}\lVert\widehat g_k(b)-g_k(b)\rVert_2.
\]
The exact decomposition
\[
 \widehat g_k(b)-g_k(b)
 =\widehat Q\{(\widehat m_k-m_k)-b(\widehat c_k-c_k)\}
  +(\widehat Q-Q_A)(m_k-bc_k)                         \tag{32}
\]
and (29)--(31), together with the population cumulant bounds following (29), imply
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta\Delta_n^2\leq K_3/n. \tag{33}
\]
There are only finitely many values of \(k\), so taking the displayed maximum changes only the constant.

\emph{Estimation and honest inversion.}
The cumulant-cancellation lemma gives, for every \(\theta\in\mathcal D_\rho\),
\[
 g_k(b)=(\beta-b)Q_Ac_k,
 \qquad g_k(\beta)=0.                                \tag{34}
\]
The objective defining \(\widehat\beta\) is no larger at its minimizer than at \(\beta\).  If \(r^\star=r\), equations (32)--(34) consequently give
\[
 |\widehat\beta-\beta|\,\lVert Q_Ac_r\rVert_2
 =\lVert g_r(\widehat\beta)\rVert_2
 \leq2\Delta_n.                                     \tag{35}
\]
Since both effects lie in \([-B,B]\), (33), (35), and the shell lower bound yield
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\mathcal M_r(\lambda_n)}
 \mathbb E_\theta(\widehat\beta-\beta)^2
 \leq K_4\min\left\{B^2,\frac{1}{n\lambda_n^2}\right\}. \tag{36}
\]
The finitely many sample sizes for which some \(n_e<R_{\max}\) are covered by increasing \(K_4\), because \(n_e\geq\underline\pi n\), the effect error is at most \(2B\), and shell strengths are uniformly bounded by (26)--(27).

Choose the deterministic calibration radius so that
\[
 t_{\alpha_0}^2\geq K_3/\alpha_0.                    \tag{37}
\]
Denote the displayed norm-sublevel set in the corrected interval definition by \(\mathcal R_n\).  This is a proof intermediate, not an additional model object.
On the event \(\Delta_n\leq t_{\alpha_0}/\sqrt n\), (34) places the true \(\beta\) in the raw inversion set \(\mathcal R_n\).  By (33), (37), and Markov's inequality, this event has probability at least \(1-\alpha_0\), uniformly over \(\mathcal D_\rho\).  The singleton fallback in the corrected definition is used only when \(\mathcal R_n\) is empty, which cannot happen on this event.  It therefore does not alter this coverage bound.  The small-sample full interval also covers.  This proves uniform honesty without inverting any influence covariance.

Each constraint defining \(\mathcal R_n\) is a sublevel set of the norm of an affine function of the scalar \(b\), hence is convex; their intersection with \([-B,B]\) is an interval.  If \(b,b'\in\mathcal R_n\), then (32)--(34) and the shell condition imply
\[
 |b-b'|\lambda_n
 \leq\lVert g_r(b)-g_r(b')\rVert_2
 \leq2\left(\frac{t_{\alpha_0}}{\sqrt n}+\Delta_n\right). \tag{38}
\]
When \(\mathcal R_n\) is empty, the corrected fallback is a singleton and has length zero.  Thus (33), (38), Cauchy--Schwarz, and the deterministic box bound give
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\mathcal M_r(\lambda_n)}
 \mathbb E_\theta\operatorname{length}(\mathcal C_n)
 \leq K_5\min\left\{B,\frac{1}{\sqrt n\lambda_n}\right\}. \tag{39}
\]
Both (35) and (38) use the true breakout order only in the analysis; the procedures maximize over all admitted orders and do not know \(r\).

\emph{A compatible full-observation lower-bound experiment.}
It remains to construct one fixed model on which (36) and (39) cannot be improved.  Choose coefficient and moment bounds with strict slack around the following compact family; this is possible because the family below is fixed and has uniformly finite source moments.  Put
\[
 J=[19/10,23/10],\quad a=3,
 \quad
 \Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}2&5\\5&14\end{pmatrix},
\]
and, for \(b\in J\), set
\[
 f_b=\frac{5-2b}{3-b},\qquad
 g_b=\frac1{3-b},\qquad z_b=b-1.                     \tag{40}
\]
All denominators and all three variances are bounded away from zero on \(J\).  If \(V_b,W_b,Z_b\) are independent centered Gaussians with these variances, then direct calculation gives
\[
 f_b+g_b=2,\qquad 3f_b+bg_b=5,\qquad
 9f_b+b^2g_b+z_b=14.                                 \tag{41}
\]
Thus
\[
 G_b=(V_b+W_b,,3V_b+bW_b+Z_b)\sim\mathcal N(0,\Sigma) \tag{42}
\]
for every \(b\in J\).

Independently, let \(L_e\) be a centered bounded-jump compound-Poisson source whose jump-\(j\) rate is increased by \(\eta\) only in environment \(e=j\leq d\), with all other rates at a common positive baseline.  Define
\[
 U_e=L_e+V_b,quad \epsilon_{t,e}=W_b,quad
 \epsilon_y=Z_b,quad \alpha=1,quad\beta=b,quad\gamma=3-b. \tag{43}
\]
Before the perturbation below,
\[
 (T_e,Y_e)=(L_e,3L_e)+G_b,                            \tag{44}
\]
so its complete law is independent of \(b\).  The calibration matrix has leading block \(\eta V_d\), and its plane is \(A=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf e_1,\ldots,\mathbf e_d\}\).

For the prescribed \(r\), let \(\operatorname{He}_r\) be the probabilists' Hermite polynomial and put
\[
 h_r(x)=e^{-x^2}\operatorname{He}_r(\sqrt3x),\qquad
 \mu_r=\frac{r!}{3^{(r+1)/2}}.                       \tag{45}
\]
If \(N\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\), the substitution \(u=\sqrt3x\) and the Rodrigues identity
\(\operatorname{He}_r(u)\phi(u)=(-1)^r\phi^{(r)}(u)\) give, by \(r\) integrations by parts,
\[
 \mathbb E[N^kh_r(N)]
 =3^{-(k+1)/2}\mathbb E[N^k\operatorname{He}_r(N)]
 =\begin{cases}0,&k<r,\\ \mu_r,&k=r.\end{cases}     \tag{46}
\]
The boundary terms vanish because a polynomial times a Gaussian density tends to zero.  Both \(h_r\) and \(h_r'\) are bounded.

Only in the spare environment \(e=d+1\), replace the density of \(W_b\) by
\[
 p_{b,\lambda}(w)=\phi_{g_b}(w)
 \left\{1+\frac{\lambda}{\mu_rg_b^{r/2}}
 h_r\!\left(\frac{w}{\sqrt{g_b}}\right)\right\}.    \tag{47}
\]
Because \(J\) and the set of orders are compact and finite, respectively, boundedness in (45) permits one \(\lambda_0>0\) for which the bracket in (47) lies in \([1/2,3/2]\) for all \(b\in J\), all admitted \(r\), and \(0<\lambda\leq\lambda_0\).  Equations (46)--(47) show separately that this is a probability density, is centered, preserves all moments below \(r\), and increases the \(r\)-th raw moment by exactly \(\lambda\).  Since all lower moments are fixed, the cumulant formula (27) shows that the \(r\)-th cumulant also increases by exactly \(\lambda\).  Gaussian domination makes the moment generating function entire and gives uniform moments of every fixed order.

The perturbation leaves \(C\) unchanged because \(r\geq d+2\), and it gives
\[
 Q_Ac_r=\lambda\mathbf e_{d+1},\qquad
 Q_Am_r=b\lambda\mathbf e_{d+1}.                     \tag{48}
\]
All lower projected contrasts vanish.  Choose once and for all a calibration gap below \(\eta\sigma_d(V_d)\), coefficient boxes containing (43), and a moment envelope strictly exceeding the compact supremum just established.  Then every law in (43)--(48), for every admitted \(r\) and \(0<\lambda\leq\lambda_0\), belongs to the same \(\mathcal M_r(\lambda)\).

We next bound the likelihood of the complete observed data.  Under the Gaussian law (42),
\[
 \mathbb E_b[W_b\mid G_b=x]=\ell_b^\top x,\qquad
 \ell_b^\top=g_b(1,b)\Sigma^{-1},                    \tag{49}
\]
and
\[
 \tau_b^2=\operatorname{Var}_b(W_b\mid G_b)
 =g_b-g_b^2(1,b)\Sigma^{-1}(1,b)^\top
 =-\frac{(b-1)(2b-5)}{3(b-3)^2}>0.                   \tag{50}
\]
The last inequality holds uniformly on \(J\).  The tilted density of \(G_b\) is
\[
 \phi_\Sigma(x)\{1+\lambda R_b(x)\},
 \quad
 R_b(x)=\frac{1}{\mu_rg_b^{r/2}}
 \mathbb E\!\left[
 h_r\!\left(\frac{\ell_b^\top x+\tau_bN}{\sqrt{g_b}}\right)
 \right].                                            \tag{51}
\]
The coefficient functions in (49)--(51) are continuously differentiable on \(J\), \(g_b\) and \(\tau_b\) are bounded away from zero, and \(h_r,h_r'\) are bounded.  Differentiating the right side of (51) under the standard-normal expectation is justified by the dominating random variable \(K(1+\lVert x\rVert+|N|)\), and gives
\[
 |R_b(x)|\leq K_6,\qquad
 |\partial_bR_b(x)|\leq K_7(1+\lVert x\rVert).       \tag{52}
\]
The constants are uniform over the finite set of \(r\).  The mean-value theorem and the finite Gaussian second moment now imply
\[
 \int\{R_b(x)-R_{b'}(x)\}^2\phi_\Sigma(x)\,dx
 \leq K_8|b-b'|^2.                                  \tag{53}
\]
After reducing \(\lambda_0\) so that \(\lambda_0K_6\leq1/2\), (51)--(53) yield
\[
 \chi^2(P_{b,\lambda}^{G},P_{b',\lambda}^{G})
 \leq2K_8\lambda^2|b-b'|^2,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{KL}(P_{b,\lambda}^{G},P_{b',\lambda}^{G})
 \leq\chi^2(P_{b,\lambda}^{G},P_{b',\lambda}^{G}).  \tag{54}
\]
The second inequality follows from \(\log x\leq x-1\).  Adding the independent \(L_e\) and applying the common map in (44) cannot increase relative entropy, chi-square divergence, or total variation.  For the first two claims, condition the likelihood ratio on the observed image and apply Jensen's inequality respectively to \(x\log x\) and \((x-1)^2\); for total variation, take suprema over inverse images.  Only observations in the spare environment change with \(b\).  Product likelihood ratios also give
\[
 1+\chi^2(P_{b,\lambda}^{,n},P_{b',\lambda}^{,n})
 \leq\exp\{K_9n\lambda^2|b-b'|^2\}.                 \tag{55}
\]

For densities \(p,q\), Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 \lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV}
 =\frac12\int|p/q-1|q
 \leq\frac12\sqrt{\chi^2(P,Q)}.                    \tag{56}
\]
Choose \(b,b+h_n\in J\), where
\[
 h_n=c\min\left\{B,\frac1{\sqrt n\lambda}\right\}, \tag{57}
\]
and choose the fixed \(c>0\) small enough that (55)--(56) make the total variation at most a number
\[
 v<\min\{1/2,1-2\alpha_0\}.                          \tag{58}
\]
For any estimator, let \(D\) be the event that it is closer to \(b\) than to \(b+h_n\).  On \(D^c\) its squared error at \(b\) is at least \(h_n^2/4\), and on \(D\) its squared error at \(b+h_n\) is at least \(h_n^2/4\).  The definition of total variation gives
\[
 \max_{j=0,1}\mathbb E_j(\widehat\beta-\beta_j)^2
 \geq\frac{h_n^2}{8}(1-v).                          \tag{59}
\]
If an interval has coverage \(1-\alpha_0\) at both laws, then under the first law the two endpoint-inclusion events have intersection probability at least \(1-2\alpha_0-v\).  On that intersection its length is at least \(h_n\), so
\[
 \mathbb E_0\operatorname{length}(\mathcal I_n)
 \geq h_n(1-2\alpha_0-v).                            \tag{60}
\]
This proves both desired lower bounds for \(0<\lambda\leq\lambda_0\), using full observed-data laws in the same shell.

For completeness, stronger nonempty shells also contain an ordinary parametric lower-bound path.  The moment bound and (27) imply a fixed \(\Lambda<\infty\) with \(\lVert Q_Ac_r\rVert\leq\Lambda\).  Take any member of a nonempty shell, retain its \(\alpha\), latent and treatment source laws, and choose a fixed \(q\in(q_0,q_1)\), \(\gamma=\alpha q\), and an invariant independent Gaussian outcome noise of sufficiently small fixed variance.  Vary \(\beta\) over a nontrivial interval inside \([-B,B]\).  None of \(C,A,r^\star\), or the shell strength changes.  In the augmented experiment observing \((U,T,Y)\), a change \(h\) in \(\beta\) changes only the conditional Gaussian mean of \(Y\) by \(hT\), and direct integration of the Gaussian likelihood ratio gives
\[
 \operatorname{KL}(P_\beta^n,P_{\beta+h}^n)
 \leq \frac{h^2}{2\sigma_y^2}\sum_e n_e\mathbb E[T_e^2]
 \leq K_{10}nh^2.                                   \tag{61}
\]
Marginalizing \(U\) can only decrease this quantity by the conditional Jensen argument used after (54).  To convert (61) to total variation without an external premise, map the two laws to the event attaining total variation.  Binary relative entropy as a function of its first probability has second derivative at least four; Taylor's theorem therefore gives \(\operatorname{KL}(P,Q)\geq2\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV}^2\).  Choosing \(h=c\min\{B,n^{-1/2}\}\) and repeating (59)--(60) gives lower bounds of orders \(\min\{B^2,n^{-1}\}\) and \(\min\{B,n^{-1/2}\}\).  Since \(\lambda_0\leq\lambda\leq\Lambda\), these are, up to fixed constants, the claimed \(\lambda\)-dependent orders.

Combining (36), (39), (59)--(61) proves the two minimax equivalences on the compatible fixed experiment.  If \(\sqrt n\lambda_n\to\infty\), (36) gives uniform mean-square consistency.  Conversely, if this divergence fails, a subsequence has \(\sqrt n\lambda_n\) bounded, and (57)--(59) give a strictly positive minimax risk on that subsequence.  No uniformly consistent estimator then exists.  This proves the final if-and-only-if assertion.

Fix \(\theta\in\mathcal N_\rho\) and put \(q=\gamma/\alpha\).  The treatment-loading lower bound ensures \(\alpha\neq0\), and the identification-frontier theorem gives
\[
 P_\theta=P_{S\theta},\qquad
 \beta(S\theta)=\beta(\theta)+q.                     \tag{62}
\]
Let \(I_n\) be any random interval having coverage at least \(1-\alpha_0\) at both structural parameters.  Under the common distribution in (62), define
\[
 A_0=\{\beta(\theta)\in I_n\},\qquad
 A_1=\{\beta(\theta)+q\in I_n\}.
\]
The two coverage inequalities and the union bound give
\[
 \mathbb P_\theta(A_0\cap A_1)
 \geq1-\mathbb P_\theta(A_0^c)-\mathbb P_\theta(A_1^c)
 \geq1-2\alpha_0.                                   \tag{63}
\]
On \(A_0\cap A_1\), an interval contains two points separated by \(|q|\), so its length is at least \(|q|\).  Since length is nonnegative, (63) yields
\[
 \mathbb E_\theta[\operatorname{length}(I_n)]
 \geq(1-2\alpha_0)|q|
 =(1-2\alpha_0)|\gamma/\alpha|,
\]
which is the asserted bound.  The condition \(\alpha_0<1/2\) makes its coefficient positive.

theorem.statement:
Yes, with a necessary qualification about what is Gaussian.  Uniformly over triangular arrays in \(\mathcal M_r(\lambda_n)\) satisfying \(\sqrt n\lambda_n\to\infty\), the stacked true-effect cumulant residuals have a first-order influence expansion whose estimated-\(A\) term, with \(C^+=(C^\top C)^{-1}C^\top\), is
\[
 -Q_A\psi^C_{e,n}C^+(m_k-\beta c_k),
\]
and their law is uniformly approximated, in bounded-Lipschitz distance, by a centered Gaussian law on the image of its possibly singular covariance.  The local cumulant-SVD estimator is characterized by the Gaussian-shift argmin relation (14); this is valid under ties, singular covariance, and the boundary \(\beta\in[-B,B]\), whereas an unconditional claim that \(\sqrt n\lambda_n(\widehat\beta-\beta)\) itself is normally distributed is false without an interiority and unique-affine-argmin condition.  A deterministic Anderson--Rubin radius satisfying \(t_{\alpha_0}^2>K_0/\alpha_0\), with \(K_0\) the uniform second-moment constant in (20), makes \(\mathcal C_n\) uniformly asymptotically honest at level \(1-\alpha_0\) without inverting the influence covariance.
theorem.proof_tex:
The structural target remains \(\beta\), while the observable estimating restrictions are the projected cumulant residuals.  Their relationship is not definitional: the cumulant cancellation identity gives, for every \(k\ge2\),
\[
 m_k-\beta c_k=\alpha^{k-1}\gamma u_k\in A,
 \qquad
 Q_A(m_k-\beta c_k)=0. \tag{22}
\]
Thus the observable residual vanishes at the causal coefficient because of source independence and the latent-profile-plane restriction.

The uniform generated-projector lemma applies to (22).  It proves equation (10), including the derivative contribution from using the same observations to form \(\widehat C\), \(\widehat Q\), \(\widehat c_k\), and \(\widehat m_k\).  It also proves the uniform Gaussian approximation (13).  Since that argument uses only characteristic functions and positive semidefiniteness, the Gaussian carrier is \(\operatorname{im}(\Sigma_n)\) when \(\Sigma_n\) is singular; no inverse or positive minimum eigenvalue has been introduced.

The local GMM and Anderson--Rubin lemma next substitutes
\[
 b=\beta+\frac{h}{\sqrt n\lambda_n}
\]
into the sample restrictions.  Its equation (18) gives the Gaussian-shift criterion with slopes \(s_{n,k}=Q_Ac_k/\lambda_n\), and the shell condition supplies the indispensable rank statement \(1\le\lVert s_{n,r}\rVert_2\le2\).  This yields tightness of \(\sqrt n\lambda_n(\widehat\beta-\beta)\) and the approximate-argmin equation (14).  That equation retains the interval constraint through \(I_n\), so it remains correct at \(\beta=-B\) or \(\beta=B\), and it does not pretend that a nonsmooth or tied argmin is linear.  When a particular submodel has a unique affine Gaussian argmin, the last implication in the lemma reduces (14) to the usual Gaussian estimator limit; otherwise (14) is the complete computable first-order law.

Finally, (22) makes the Anderson--Rubin statistic at the true causal value exactly the norm-max statistic treated in (20).  Choosing \(t_{\alpha_0}^2>K_0/\alpha_0\) and applying (21) proves uniform asymptotic coverage at least \(1-\alpha_0\).  The calibration is conservative but fully explicit and remains valid when all or part of the Gaussian covariance collapses.  Exact similarity from a single law-independent scalar radius is not asserted: it would require a covariance-dependent quantile and a continuity condition at that quantile.  This proves the stated qualified affirmative answer.
theorem.justification: This resolves the open proof boundary by giving the same-sample projector correction, a singular Gaussian carrier, the precise Gaussian-driven argmin law, and an explicit uniformly honest Anderson--Rubin calibration.
theorem.gap: The result proves the generated-projector expansion directly and distinguishes the Gaussian moment process from a generally nonsmooth estimator argmin, avoiding an unsupported universal normality claim.
theorem.consumer: The expansion and calibration permit singularity-safe uncertainty quantification for weak environmental cumulant flags.

Fix \(r\in\{d+2,\ldots,R_{\max}\}\).  For every triangular array in \(\mathcal M_r(\lambda_n)\), write the observation in environment \(e\) as \(W_{e,i}=(T_{e,i},Y_{e,i})\), put \(C^+=(C^\top C)^{-1}C^\top\), and put \(h_k=m_k-\beta c_k\).  There are centered first-projection arrays \(\psi^C_{e,n}(W_{e,i})\), \(\psi^c_{e,k,n}(W_{e,i})\), and \(\psi^m_{e,k,n}(W_{e,i})\) such that, simultaneously for \(d+2\le k\le R_{\max}\),
\[
 \sqrt n\,\widehat Q(\widehat m_k-\beta\widehat c_k)
 =Z_{n,k}+o_{\mathbb P}(1),
 \qquad
 Z_{n,k}=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}\pi_e^{-1}\zeta_{e,k,n}(W_{e,i}),
\]
uniformly over the array, where
\[
 \zeta_{e,k,n}
 =Q_A\bigl(\psi^m_{e,k,n}-\beta\psi^c_{e,k,n}
       -\psi^C_{e,n}C^+h_k\bigr).
\]
The remainder is uniform in probability, and the stacked vector \(Z_n=(Z_{n,k}:d+2\le k\le R_{\max})\) satisfies
\[
 d_{\mathrm{BL}}\!\left(\mathcal L(Z_n),N(0,\Sigma_n)\right)\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad
 \Sigma_n=\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\pi_e^{-1}
 \mathbb E\bigl[\zeta_{e,n}\zeta_{e,n}^{\top}\bigr],
\]
uniformly.  This conclusion allows \(\Sigma_n\) to be singular; \(N(0,\Sigma_n)\) is then the Gaussian law supported on \(\operatorname{im}(\Sigma_n)\).  The term \(-Q_A\psi^C_{e,n}C^+h_k\) is the same-sample estimated-\(A\) correction.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Fix a triangular array and suppress its \(n\)-index where this creates no ambiguity.  We derive every part of the expansion.

First, the coefficient restrictions in the ambient class give \(\lvert\alpha\rvert\le a_1\), \(\lvert\beta\rvert\le B\), and \(\lvert\gamma\rvert\le a_1q_1\).  From the structural equations and the elementary inequality
\[
 \lvert x_1+\cdots+x_j\rvert^s\le j^{s-1}
 \sum_{a=1}^j\lvert x_a\rvert^s
\]
for \(s\ge1\), the source moment envelope therefore implies a constant \(K_W<\infty\), depending only on the fixed envelopes, for which
\[
 \sup_n\max_{e\in\mathcal E}
 \mathbb E\!\left[\lVert W_{e,1}\rVert^{2R_{\max}+\delta}\right]
 \le K_W. \tag{1}
\]
Balanced shares imply \(n_e\ge \underline\pi n\), so all environment sample sizes tend to infinity uniformly.

For random variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_k\), the order-\(k\) cumulant is the finite polynomial
\[
 \kappa_k(X_1,\ldots,X_k)
 =\sum_{\mathcal P}
 (\lvert\mathcal P\rvert-1)!(-1)^{\lvert\mathcal P\rvert-1}
 \prod_{D\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E\!\left[\prod_{j\in D}X_j\right], \tag{2}
\]
where the sum is over the set partitions \(\mathcal P\) of \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\).  Replacing each product of expectations in (2) by its symmetrized average over distinct sample indices gives the stipulated unbiased cumulant statistic.  Consequently each coordinate of \(\widehat C\), \(\widehat c_k\), and \(\widehat m_k\) is a finite linear combination, with coefficients depending only on \(R_{\max}\), of symmetric \(U\)-statistics of orders at most \(R_{\max}\).

For completeness, let \(U_s(g)\) be one such statistic and let \(g_j\) be the centered \(j\)-variable projection obtained by expanding \(g\) after successively subtracting all conditional expectations involving fewer than \(j\) arguments.  Inclusion--exclusion gives the exact identity
\[
 U_s(g)-\mathbb Eg
 =\frac1{n_e}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}\psi_g(W_{e,i})
  +\sum_{j=2}^s {s\choose j}U_j(g_j),
 \qquad
 \psi_g(w)=s\bigl(\mathbb E[g(w,W_2,\ldots,W_s)]-\mathbb Eg\bigr). \tag{3}
\]
Every \(g_j\) in the second sum has conditional mean zero in each argument.  Hence two summands indexed by different unordered \(j\)-tuples have zero covariance unless the tuples coincide.  It follows directly that
\[
 \mathbb E\bigl[U_j(g_j)^2\bigr]
 \le {n_e\choose j}^{-1}\mathbb E[g_j^2]
 \le K n_e^{-j}, \tag{4}
\]
where (1) supplies the last uniform bound because the kernels have total polynomial degree at most \(R_{\max}\).  There are only finitely many coordinates and partitions.  Stacking (3), using (4), and inserting the signs defining environment contrasts therefore yields
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat C-C)
 =\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_e\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}\pi_e^{-1}\psi^C_e(W_{e,i})+o_{L^2}(1), \tag{5}
\]
and analogous equations for \(\sqrt n(\widehat c_k-c_k)\) and \(\sqrt n(\widehat m_k-m_k)\), uniformly in \(e\) and \(k\).  With
\[
 \nu=\min\left\{1,\frac{\delta}{R_{\max}}\right\}>0,
\]
equation (1) and the polynomial degree bound also give
\[
 \sup_{n,e}\mathbb E\!\left[
 \lVert\psi^C_e\rVert^{2+\nu}
 +\sum_{k=2}^{R_{\max}}
 \bigl(\lVert\psi^c_{e,k}\rVert^{2+\nu}
       +\lVert\psi^m_{e,k}\rVert^{2+\nu}\bigr)
 \right]<\infty, \tag{6}
\]
because \((2+\nu)R_{\max}\le2R_{\max}+\delta\).

We next expand the spectral projector.  Put \(P_C=CC^+\), so \(Q_A=I-P_C\).  If \(H\) is a perturbation of \(C\), expansion of
\[
 \bigl((C+H)^\top(C+H)\bigr)^{-1}
\]
around \((C^\top C)^{-1}\), followed by multiplication on the left and right by \(C+H\) and \((C+H)^\top\), gives
\[
 P_{C+H}-P_C
 =Q_AHC^+ +(Q_AHC^+)^\top+R_C(H),
 \qquad
 \lVert R_C(H)\rVert\le K_P\lVert H\rVert^2. \tag{7}
\]
To verify the bound, write \(G=C^\top C\) and
\(D=C^\top H+H^\top C+H^\top H\).  The identity
\[
 (G+D)^{-1}=G^{-1}-G^{-1}DG^{-1}
 +G^{-1}DG^{-1}D(G+D)^{-1}
\]
shows that all omitted terms are quadratic in \(H\).  The calibration gap gives \(\lVert G^{-1}\rVert\le\kappa_0^{-2}\); (1) bounds \(\lVert C\rVert\), and on the event \(\lVert H\rVert\le\kappa_0/2\) the last inverse is uniformly bounded.  Thus the constant \(K_P\) in (7) is uniform.  Equation (5) makes that event have probability tending to one and gives \(\lVert H\rVert=O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2})\).  Since \(\widehat Q=I-P_{\widehat C}\), (7) consequently implies
\[
 \widehat Q-Q_A
 =-Q_A(\widehat C-C)C^+
  -\bigl(Q_A(\widehat C-C)C^+\bigr)^\top
  +o_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2}). \tag{8}
\]

By the cumulant cancellation identity, \(h_k=m_k-\beta c_k\in A=\operatorname{col}(C)\), hence \(Q_Ah_k=0\).  Moreover,
\[
 \bigl(Q_A(\widehat C-C)C^+\bigr)^\top h_k
 =C^{+\top}(\widehat C-C)^\top Q_Ah_k=0. \tag{9}
\]
Combining (5), (8), and (9), and observing that the product of two root-\(n\) estimation errors is \(O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1})\), gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sqrt n\,\widehat Q(\widehat m_k-\beta\widehat c_k)
 & =\sqrt n\,Q_A\bigl[(\widehat m_k-m_k)
       -\beta(\widehat c_k-c_k)\bigr]
    -\sqrt n\,Q_A(\widehat C-C)C^+h_k+o_{\mathbb P}(1)\\
 & =\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_e\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}\pi_e^{-1}
 Q_A\bigl(\psi^m_{e,k}-\beta\psi^c_{e,k}-\psi^C_eC^+h_k\bigr)(W_{e,i})
 +o_{\mathbb P}(1),
 \end{aligned} \tag{10}
\]
which is the asserted same-sample correction and proves the influence expansion.

It remains to establish a Gaussian approximation without assuming invertibility.  Let \(\zeta_{e,n}\) denote the stack in (10).  By (6), boundedness of \(Q_A\), boundedness of \(C^+\) from the gap, and boundedness of \(h_k\),
\[
 \sup_{n,e}\mathbb E\lVert\zeta_{e,n}\rVert^{2+\nu}<\infty. \tag{11}
\]
For the independent summands \(X_{e,i,n}=n^{-1/2}\pi_e^{-1}\zeta_{e,n}(W_{e,i})\), balanced shares and (11) imply
\[
 \sum_e\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}\mathbb E\lVert X_{e,i,n}\rVert^{2+\nu}
 \le K n^{-\nu/2}\longrightarrow0. \tag{12}
\]
For every fixed vector \(t\), Taylor expansion of \(\exp(i t^\top X_{e,i,n})\) through order two has a remainder bounded by \(K_t\mathbb E\lVert X_{e,i,n}\rVert^{2+\nu}\).  Multiplying the characteristic functions and using (12) therefore gives
\[
 \mathbb E\exp(i t^\top Z_n)
 -\exp\left(-\tfrac12t^\top\Sigma_nt\right)\longrightarrow0. \tag{13}
\]
The matrices \(\Sigma_n\) lie in a compact bounded subset of the positive semidefinite cone by (11).  If uniform bounded-Lipschitz convergence failed, one could choose a violating sequence and then a subsequence with \(\Sigma_n\to\Sigma\).  Equation (13) on that subsequence gives convergence to the characteristic function \(\exp(-t^\top\Sigma t/2)\), while \(N(0,\Sigma_n)\) converges to the same law.  Approximation of bounded Lipschitz functions by finite linear combinations of Fourier exponentials on a large compact set, with the tails controlled by the common second-moment bound, then forces the bounded-Lipschitz distance to zero, a contradiction.  This argument never divides by an eigenvalue of \(\Sigma_n\); it therefore includes every singular covariance and completes the proof.

added_lemmas.statement:
Under the conclusion of the uniform generated-projector expansion, define \(s_{n,k}=Q_Ac_k/\lambda_n\), let \(Z_n=(Z_{n,k})_{k=d+2}^{R_{\max}}\), and set
\[
 \mathfrak L_n(h;z)=\max_{d+2\le k\le R_{\max}}
 \lVert z_k-hs_{n,k}\rVert_2,
 \qquad
 I_n=\sqrt n\lambda_n[-B-\beta,B-\beta].
\]
If \(\sqrt n\lambda_n\to\infty\), then, uniformly over \(\mathcal M_r(\lambda_n)\),
\[
 \sqrt n\lambda_n(\widehat\beta-\beta)=O_{\mathbb P}(1)
\]
and, with \(\widehat h_n=\sqrt n\lambda_n(\widehat\beta-\beta)\),
\[
 \mathfrak L_n(\widehat h_n;Z_n)
 \le \inf_{h\in I_n}\mathfrak L_n(h;Z_n)+o_{\mathbb P}(1). \tag{14}
\]
Thus the first-order law of the possibly nonsmooth estimator is the argmin functional of a Gaussian-shift criterion, with the box constraint retained; an ordinary Gaussian limit follows only when that argmin functional is locally unique and affine.  In addition, there is a finite constant \(K_0\), depending only on the fixed model envelopes, such that every deterministic choice satisfying \(t_{\alpha_0}^2>K_0/\alpha_0\) yields
\[
 \liminf_{n\to\infty}\ \inf_{\theta\in\mathcal M_r(\lambda_n)}
 \mathbb P_\theta\bigl(\beta\in\mathcal C_n\bigr)\ge1-\alpha_0. \tag{15}
\]
This calibration remains valid for singular influence covariance and requires no generalized inverse.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
For \(b=\beta+h/(\sqrt n\lambda_n)\), linearity in \(b\) and the first helper lemma give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sqrt n\,\widehat Q(\widehat m_k-b\widehat c_k)
 &=\sqrt n\,\widehat Q(\widehat m_k-\beta\widehat c_k)
   -\frac{h}{\lambda_n}\widehat Q\widehat c_k\\
 &=Z_{n,k}-h\frac{Q_Ac_k}{\lambda_n}
   -\frac{h}{\lambda_n}(\widehat Q\widehat c_k-Q_Ac_k)
   +o_{\mathbb P}(1). 
 \end{aligned} \tag{16}
\]
Equations (5) and (8) in the preceding proof, applied to \(\widehat c_k\), imply
\[
 \max_{2\le k\le R_{\max}}
 \lVert\widehat Q\widehat c_k-Q_Ac_k\rVert_2
 =O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2}) \tag{17}
\]
uniformly.  Therefore, for each fixed \(H<\infty\), \(\sqrt n\lambda_n\to\infty\) turns (16) into
\[
 \sup_{\lvert h\rvert\le H}\max_k
 \left\lVert
 \sqrt n\,\widehat Q(\widehat m_k-b\widehat c_k)
 -(Z_{n,k}-hs_{n,k})
 \right\rVert_2=o_{\mathbb P}(1). \tag{18}
\]

The defining shell inequalities give \(1\le\lVert s_{n,r}\rVert_2\le2\).  At \(h=0\), the sample criterion multiplied by \(\sqrt n\) is \(O_{\mathbb P}(1)\), because \(Z_n=O_{\mathbb P}(1)\) uniformly by its common second-moment bound.  At the minimizing \(\widehat h_n\), its value is no larger.  Applying the reverse triangle inequality to the \(r\)-th component of (16), and using (17), gives
\[
 \lvert\widehat h_n\rvert
 \le O_{\mathbb P}(1)
 +\frac{\lvert\widehat h_n\rvert}{\sqrt n\lambda_n}O_{\mathbb P}(1). \tag{19}
\]
The last random coefficient is smaller than one half with probability tending uniformly to one, so it can be absorbed into the left side.  Hence \(\widehat h_n=O_{\mathbb P}(1)\).  On a compact interval containing \(\widehat h_n\) with arbitrarily high uniform probability, (18) and the minimizing property of \(\widehat\beta\) yield (14).  Because changing every block \(z_k\) by at most \(a\) changes \(\mathfrak L_n(h;z)\) by at most \(a\), the bounded-Lipschitz Gaussian approximation for \(Z_n\) transfers to every bounded Lipschitz functional of the local criterion.  If the Gaussian argmin is unique and separated, the elementary argmin implication
\[
 \sup_{\lvert h\rvert\le H}\lvert f_n(h)-f(h)\rvert\to0,
 \quad
 \inf_{\lvert h-h_0\rvert\ge\varepsilon}f(h)>f(h_0)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \mathop{\rm argmin}f_n\to h_0
\]
gives the corresponding estimator distribution.  If uniqueness fails or \(\beta\) lies on the boundary, (14), rather than an unjustified normal law, is the valid first-order characterization.

For coverage, define
\[
 S_n=\max_{d+2\le k\le R_{\max}}
 \left\lVert\sqrt n\,\widehat Q(\widehat m_k-\beta\widehat c_k)\right\rVert_2.
\]
The first helper lemma and the moment bounds give a finite \(K_0\) for which
\[
 \limsup_n\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal M_r(\lambda_n)}
 \mathbb E_\theta[S_n^2]\le K_0. \tag{20}
\]
To check the bound without demanding fourth moments, use (5) and the deterministic projector bounds
\[
 \lVert\widehat Q-Q_A\rVert\le2,
 \qquad
 \lVert\widehat Q-Q_A\rVert\le K\lVert\widehat C-C\rVert
 \quad\text{when }\lVert\widehat C-C\rVert\le\kappa_0/2.
\]
The second bound follows from (7), while Markov's inequality and (5) show that the complementary event has probability \(O(n^{-1})\).  Consequently \(n\mathbb E\lVert(\widehat Q-Q_A)h_k\rVert^2\) is bounded.  The other part, \(\sqrt n\widehat Q[(\widehat m_k-m_k)-\beta(\widehat c_k-c_k)]\), has bounded second moment by (3)--(6) and \(\lVert\widehat Q\rVert\le1\).  This proves (20).  If the displayed inversion set in the definition of \(\mathcal C_n\) is empty, the prescribed fallback \([-B,B]\) contains \(\beta\).  Otherwise, failure to cover \(\beta\) implies \(S_n>t_{\alpha_0}\).  Hence Markov's inequality, proved here by
\[
 \mathbb E[S_n^2]\ge t_{\alpha_0}^2
 \mathbb P(S_n>t_{\alpha_0}),
\]
and (20) give
\[
 \limsup_n\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal M_r(\lambda_n)}
 \mathbb P_\theta(\beta\notin\mathcal C_n)
 \le \frac{K_0}{t_{\alpha_0}^2}<\alpha_0. \tag{21}
\]
This proves (15).  Neither (20) nor (21) uses the rank of \(\Sigma_n\), which proves singularity robustness.
added_lemmas.justification: This lemma converts the corrected moment expansion into a computable local argmin law and a covariance-inversion-free coverage guarantee.
added_lemmas.gap: A Gaussian moment process need not produce an ordinary Gaussian estimator when the max-norm criterion ties or the effect lies on the compact boundary.
added_lemmas.consumer: The OEQ resolution uses this lemma to state the sharp form of the estimator approximation and Anderson--Rubin calibration.
